subject: babaYagaHut
pitch:
Category: Diorama.
Subject: Baba Yaga's hut on chicken legs.
Style: Slavic folk art.

spec.name: Baba Yaga's Hut on Chicken Legs
spec.description: A Slavic folk-art diorama: a painted log izba with carved bargeboards and a horse-head ridge, standing on two giant scaly chicken legs inside a ring of glowing-eyed skull fence posts.
spec.layout:
STYLE: Slavic folk art (lubok, Khokhloma, painted carved wood). Every motif is a bold flat-colour shape, chunky and slightly exaggerated, with a dark ink (#1b1410) outline or underlay behind the main colour and small cream or yellow highlight dots on top. Colours are red, cobalt blue, sun yellow and orange on warm wood, with green foliage and cream accents. The repeated motifs are (1) the SUN ROSETTE: a yellow disc with 8 orange petals and a red ring, with a cream centre dot; (2) the TOOTH TRIM: a row of alternating red and blue triangles; (3) SCALLOPS: half-round cut-outs on carved boards; (4) the ROOSTER/TULIP: a stylised bird or flower of three flat petals. Reuse all four on the hut, door, gate posts and props.
SILHOUETTE (+Z is the front): the model is a round diorama base about 6.8 m across. At the centre a log hut about 2.3 m wide (x) by 2.7 m deep (z) stands on two huge chicken legs. The sill underside is at y=2.0, the wall top at y=3.55, the ridge at y=4.64, and a horse-head ornament and chimney reach about y=5.0. The legs are digitigrade: the thigh runs forward-down to a forward knee, the shin runs backward-down to the hock, and the tarsus runs forward-down to a foot with three forward toes and one rear toe. The legs sit at x=+-0.7 and the feet at x=+-0.75, z=0.25. The hut faces +Z with a door in the centre of the front wall, a small porch platform, and a steep ladder-stair going down to the ground at z=2.75. The roof is a steep gable with its ridge along Z, so the gable triangle faces front and back. It has fish-scale shingles and carved bargeboards. A carved horse head (konyok) sits on each end of the ridge, and a brick chimney with smoke is on the model-right roof slope.
GROUND: the base disc is r=3.4 with its grass top at y=0.15. A fence of skull-topped stakes forms a ring at r=3.0 over azimuth 40 to 320 degrees (azimuth 0 is +Z, 90 is +X), so the front is open and the path runs through. Two taller carved gate posts stand at az=+-40 degrees, which is (+-1.93, z=2.30). Birch trees stand behind the hut, with a mortar, pestle and broom, mushrooms, folk flowers and a black cat as small dressing. The feet stand on the base top. The only things that touch the model floor y=0 are the base disc and the fence stakes. The hut and legs rest on y=0.15.
Coordinate convention: +X is the model's left; mirrored parts use for s of [1,-1], with s=1 the left (+X). Rest pose: legs standing, door closed.

parts.builds: Both giant chicken legs, mirrored (L at +X, R at -X), built from the rig. Build them as a chain through hip, knee, ankle and foot (a limb/IK solve landing the foot on footL/footR, or sweeps through the joint positions), with smooth skin sweeps. THIGH: a fat feathered 'trouser' of radius about 0.28 at the hip tapering to 0.17 at the knee. It is a base sweep in featherA covered with 14-20 overlapping broad feather blades (flat extruded leaf shapes, or cards/spikes) in a root-to-tip featherA to featherB palette, pointing down and back, with a ruff of longer feather blades round the knee. KNEE and HOCK: chunky knuckle blocks in scaleDark. TARSUS (shin and lower leg): scaly yellow, radius about 0.11 at the hock tapering to 0.09, in scaleYellow. It carries a row of overlapping scale plates (small flat boxes or rounded plates, scaleDark) down the front, with a spur (an ink cone) at the back of the hock. Each hock gets a folk 'bracelet': a red (folkRed) ring sweep with 6-8 tiny cream dots round it. TOES: four per leg, one sweep each (radius 0.08 tapering to 0.05) along the toe joints toeX1..toeX4 (three forward, spread outward, centre and inward, plus one rear toe). Each has 2-3 knuckle bumps in scaleDark, a toe pad underside, and a long curved ink talon (a cone or curved sweep, 0.16-0.2 m) at the tip, which rests on the ground. The rear toe is shorter with a bigger spur-claw. Add a few lumps of earth (earth colour) over the toes and a small yellow-orange dot motif. At the top of each thigh a rounded hip cap in featherA tucks under the hut's sill at hipL/hipR (y up to 2.0). Use the joints hipX, kneeX, ankleX, footX, toeX1..4 and give the leg chain role 'leg' and the toes role 'digit'.
parts.attaches: Hips at mounts hipL/hipR just under hutSillBottom (y 2.0). The feet land on footL/footR with toe undersides sinking slightly into groundTop (y 0.15). Parented to the hut joint.

parts.builds: The log cabin walls, floor beams, front door, windows, porch and stair. WALLS: a core box (x +-1.15, z +-1.35, y 2.15 to 3.55) in logDark so there are no gaps. On the front and back walls, horizontal log cylinders (radius 0.1, 8 sides, logWarm) at y=2.25+0.2i for i 0..6, spanning x +-1.3 so they stick out past the corners. On the side walls, logs at y=2.35+0.2i for i 0..5 spanning z +-1.5. Each log end gets a logEnd disc with a ring/annual-ring detail (a smaller darker logDark disc and a centre dot). Bands of moss (grassTop) lie on the top of the highest logs. SILL: two heavy sill beams (box, logDark) under the floor at y 2.0 to 2.15 spanning the full depth, with carved scallop ends. A wall top plate in logDark at y 3.45 to 3.55. FRONT DOOR at doorCentre: a doorway 0.72 wide by 1.2 tall (y 2.15 to 3.35) with a carved frame (platband: folkRed boards, tooth trim of red/blue triangles up the sides, a folkBlue lintel with a cream sun rosette above). The door itself rides joint 'door' (hinge at doorHinge, x=-0.36, swinging about the vertical axis) and is closed in rest pose: planks in logWarm with logDark seams, iron-look ink hinge straps, a folkYellow tree-of-life or tulip motif (three flat petals on a stalk) in ink/folkRed/folkYellow, and a round ring handle in ink. WINDOWS: at windowL1, L2, R1 and R2 on the side walls, each 0.5 wide by 0.55 tall, with a windowGlow pane (glow) divided by a cream cross, and a carved platband frame in folkRed with a scalloped top board in folkBlue with yellow dots. Painted shutters in folkBlue with a cream tulip motif sit open at each side. PORCH: a platform (x +-0.6, z 1.35 to 1.95, y 2.0 to 2.15) in logWarm with plank lines, and two corner posts with carved onion-top finials at z 1.9, x +-0.55, rising to y 2.95, joined by a folkRed railing. STAIR: a steep ladder-stair from stairTop (0, 2.0, 1.95) down to stairBottom (0, 0.15, 2.75), 0.7 wide, with two logDark stringers and 8-9 logWarm treads, and tooth trim (red/blue) on the stringer outer faces. Add a hanging folk towel (a cream rectangle with red trim and tooth ends) beside the door, and a few yellow dot studs on the sill.
parts.attaches: Sits on the hut joint at hutSillBottom (y 2.0) above the legs' hip caps. The wall top plate at wallTop (y 3.55) is where the roof starts. The stair foot lands on stairBottom at groundTop y 0.15. Door rides joint 'door'.

parts.builds: The steep gable roof and everything above wallTop (y 3.55). The roof surface passes through (x=+-1.15, y=3.55) and the ridge (0, 4.64), i.e. a slope of 0.95. It continues to the eave at x=+-1.75, y=2.98. It runs z from -1.85 to +1.85, so the gable ends overhang. Each slope is a layer of boards (0.1 thick) with 8-9 rows of fish-scale shingles (scalloped rounded extruded tiles, about 0.22 wide), alternating shingleA and shingleB per tile, rows overlapping like scales. Every 4th row has a row of tiles tinted folkRed for a folk accent, and the eave row is trimmed with cream dots. RIDGE: a heavy round log along z at the ridge in logDark, with a row of yellow dots on top. GABLE INFILL: triangle of vertical planks (logWarm, thin boxes with logDark seams) at the front (z=1.35) and back (z=-1.35), from y 3.55 to 4.64. BARGEBOARDS (carved gable-edge boards): on both slopes at the front and back, a 0.22-wide carved board in folkRed with a scalloped lower edge, a row of blue circles and a sun-yellow dot in each scallop, plus a cream tooth-trim line along the top. FRONT GABLE: a round window at gableWindowFront (0.4 diameter, windowGlow glow pane, folkBlue ring, a sun rosette of 8 yellow-orange petals around it) and a hanging carved pendant 'prichelina' under the peak (folkBlue shield with a cream sun and a red tooth edge). KONYOK: a carved horse head in profile on each end of the ridge (konyokFront at z=1.85, konyokBack at z=-1.85), both facing outward, about 0.4 m. They are extruded profile outlines in logWarm with a folkRed mane scalloped in blades, a cream eye with an ink pupil, a folkBlue bridle, and yellow dots on the neck. CHIMNEY at chimneyBase (x=-0.6): a brick stack 0.35 square rising to y 4.95 with brick courses (alternating red/orange brick colours using folkRed and folkOrange boxes), a cream cap slab, and 3-4 smoke puffs (low-poly spheres, cream and stone tinted, getting bigger and rising to y 5.3) drifting back.
parts.attaches: The roof underside meets the wall top plate at wallTop (y 3.55). The gable infill rests on the front and back wall faces (z=+-1.35). The horse heads sit on the ridge ends konyokFront/konyokBack. All on the hut joint.

parts.builds: The diorama ground and the skull fence. BASE: a 16-sided disc of radius 3.4 whose top is at y=0.15 (grassTop, with a slightly darker ring of 3-5 irregular lighter/darker flat patches in green), and an earth side wall from y=0 to 0.15 in earth, with 10-12 small stone blocks (stone) round the rim. A packed-earth path (earth, a flat low shape) runs from stairBottom (0, 0.15, 2.75) out through the gate gap to z=3.3, with 4-5 flat stone slabs (stone). A few grass tufts and patches of moss round the legs' feet. SKULL FENCE: about 30 stakes at radius 3.0 from azimuth 40 to 320 degrees (0 is +Z, 90 is +X), evenly spaced (about 0.48 m apart), at heights alternating 1.1 and 1.3, each a sharpened cylindrical post (6-8 sides) in logDark with a logWarm cap ring. Each carries a skull on top: cranium (low-poly sphere, bone), a separate jaw box (bone), a nose (ink triangle), two big eye sockets (ink spheres) with glowEye glow inside (use the glow kit), and a row of small teeth. A few skulls tilt slightly (+-8 degrees). Between the stakes at y 0.55 runs a log rail (logDark). Every 5th stake has a folkRed band with cream dots. GATE POSTS at gatePostL/gatePostR (az=+-40 degrees, i.e. (+-1.93, z=2.3)): taller (1.5 m) carved posts in logWarm, each with a folkRed tooth-trim band, a folkBlue sun-rosette disc panel facing the path, and a bigger skull on top (cranium plus separate jaw, glowEye eyes), and a folkYellow pointed cap between skull and post. Keep this part simpler than the hut.
parts.attaches: Base top at groundTop (y 0.15). The hut's stair foot at stairBottom and the legs' feet at footL/footR rest on it. The fence centre is fenceCentre. Rides joint 'base'.

parts.builds: Dressing standing on groundTop (y 0.15), keeping out of the hut-legs zone (|x|<1.45, -0.8<z<1.5) and the path (|x|<0.6, z>1.9). BIRCH TREES: two birches at birchBackL (2.4, -1.4) and birchBackR (-2.35, -1.0), about 4.7 m tall. Each has a faceted tapered trunk (birchWhite, 6-7 sides, radius 0.14 to 0.07), ink dash marks (small flat boxes) round the trunk, 4-5 branches (thin sweeps, birchWhite) and a folk-art canopy of 8-12 flat leaf-shaped extruded blobs/chunky low-poly clumps in green, some in folkYellow, with tiny cream dots; there is a red ribbon with tooth ends tied to one branch. MORTAR AND PESTLE at mortarSpot (2.0, 0.15, 1.5): a flared stone mortar (lathe, stone) about 0.8 wide and 0.55 tall with a folkRed painted band with cream dots and a sun rosette on the front; a long pestle (logWarm, red-capped) leaning out of it at about 25 degrees; and a broom (logDark handle, a bundle of twig blades in logWarm/logDark tied with a folkRed band) leaning against the mortar. MUSHROOMS: 6-9 fly agaric (red cap folkRed, cream dots, cream stem) in two clusters at the front left and back right, 0.1-0.25 high. FOLK FLOWERS: 8-10 stylised flowers (3-5 flat petal blades in folkRed, folkBlue and folkYellow, a yellow centre dot, a green stalk and two leaf blades) scattered round the base inside the fence. A few grass tufts, 3-4 stones and a stump. BLACK CAT at catSpot (0.42, 2.15, 1.65) on the porch, sitting facing front: an ink body, head, two ears, a curved tail, and glowEye eyes (glow). A raven perched on the left gate post top? No: put the raven (ink body, wedge beak in folkYellow) on a fence stake at azimuth 270 degrees. Keep each small and in the folk-art flat style with ink outline layers.
parts.attaches: All feet on groundTop (y 0.15) except the cat, which sits on floorTop (y 2.15) of the porch at catSpot. Ground items ride the 'base' joint and the cat rides 'hut'.

calls.reasoning:
I'm sketching out the spec for Baba Yaga's hut on chicken legs as a Slavic folk art diorama, thinking through real-world proportions like a 2.4m wide hut and 1.6m tall legs, plus a small ground base to anchor the scene, before structuring it as JSON for the team to build.

I picture the hut as a log cabin with a steep gabled roof, carved bargeboards, a horse-head ridge ornament, red-and-blue window platbands, and a descending ladder-step porch, all perched atop two scaly bird legs with three-toed talons. I'm also considering adding the iconic skull-fence detail around a round earth base, and starting to define the skeleton hierarchy—root joint, hip/knee/ankle chains for each leg, and toe digits—to rig the chicken legs properly.

Now I'm working out exact proportions: base disc radius, hut body dimensions, roof height with the carved ridge ornament, and where the leg joints (hip, knee, ankle, toes) should sit relative to the floor and ground plane so the whole structure reads as balanced and proportioned.

Adding a small chimney on the roof back, bringing total height to 5.0 with legs at 2.0 and hut at 3.0 — a bit oversized but stylistically fine. For the front door, I'm placing it high on the +Z wall with a porch platform and a stairway leading down to the ground, making sure the steps clear the leg positions at x ±0.7.

Now I'm working out the leg anatomy — thighs running from hip down-forward to a knee, then an ankle angled backward like a real bird's leg, with scaly yellow skin as the classic depiction.

Checking segment lengths come out close to target and adjusting ankle/foot positions, then sketching front toe joints splaying forward-out from the foot for a natural stance.

I'm mapping out the remaining three toes per side with one going back as a rear spur, keeping each toe as a single joint parented to the foot, then mirroring everything for the right side with negated x-coordinates. I'm settling on joint naming (hipL/kneeL/ankleL/footL plus toeL1-4, mirrored R), totaling 17 joints, and considering whether to add hinge joints for a door and shutters.

Now I'm planning the part budget breakdown, starting with the chicken legs as the first part group covering both legs with feather trousers, scales, and talons, aiming to stay within an overall parts budget while deciding whether to include chimney smoke puffs as a separate detail.

For the legs, I'm deciding whether to mark them as floor-resting or let them sink slightly into the base disc, concluding legs should be floor:false with toes sinking a bit into the base, which itself is floor:true. Then I move on to the second part group: the hut body, covering log walls, foundation sill, corner log ends, door, windows, shutters, porch, and steps.

For the porch and steps, I'm working out the bounding box dimensions and deciding the steps should extend down to near ground level as part of the hutBody group rather than a separate grounds part, checking that its box doesn't overlap the legs since they occupy different x ranges. Then I start outlining the third part: a steep gable roof with rows of wooden shingles, carved bargeboards, konyok ridge-end carvings, and a ridge log.

Now I'm adding details to the roof group — chimney, smoke, a small round gable window with a sun emblem, and pendant ornaments — and setting its bounding box, then moving to the base/fence group: a ground disc with grass, moss, paths, and a skull fence with glowing eyes, mushrooms, and pebbles, with its own bounding box and floor flag. I'm placing the fence posts in an arc around the back and sides at a set radius, leaving an open gateway in front flanked by gateposts.

I'm working out proportions for the front porch steps and gate so they don't feel cramped against the fence — widening the base radius slightly, pulling the fence radius in, and shortening the stairs into a steep ladder-style stoop rising from near ground level up to the porch.

I'm also thinking about adding a fifth part to the scene for forest dressing — birch trees behind the hut, fly agaric mushroom clusters for that folk-art touch, and Baba Yaga's mortar and pestle with a broom leaning against the fence, keeping these separate from the base and fence group to balance the composition.

I'm settling on five total parts (legs, hut body, roof, base/fence, and props), sizing the whole diorama around 6.8 x 5.1 x 6.8, and placing tall birch trees in the back corners around height 4.4-4.6 with stylized leaf clusters to keep everything within bounds.

Checking the positions and radii so the trees stay clear of the fence and don't collide with the hut's roof overhang, adjusting trunk placement until the canopies sit just outside the eaves without clipping through.

Now I'm settling on a folk-art color palette inspired by Khokhloma style — bold reds, deep blue, ochre yellow, cream white, green, black, and warm wood tones — to use for painted carvings with sun rosettes, cockerel motifs, scalloped trim, and repeating triangle patterns, keeping the total palette capped around 24 colors.

Still refining the palette...

Trimming the palette down by merging similar shades and dropping redundant ones, I get it to 23 colors total, reusing ink for talon and logDark for the door. Now I'm moving on to planning the mounts.

Working out the vertical layout of the hut: sill bottom at y=2.0, floor top at 2.15, wall top/eaves around 3.45-3.55, and ridge near 4.65-4.75. I'm adjusting the roof pitch steeper, aiming for roughly a 35°+ slope with the eave overhanging and ridge rising about 1.4 units over a 1.7 run.

Let me try a gentler slope of 0.95, giving a ridge height around 4.64 and eave tip near 2.98, for a more moderate 43.5° pitch — more reasonable for the roof proportions.

Now I'm laying out the overall hut structure: walls spanning roughly 2.3 by 2.7 meters, with protruding corner log ends and roof overhang extending further out. I'm assigning ownership of parts — the roof component handles the gable infill triangles (with vertical planks and a round sun window), while the hut body owns the walls up to the top plate log. Then I'm sketching out the porch platform dimensions as the next structural piece.

I'm deciding to skip front windows since the spacing is too tight with the door, keeping only the side windows for simplicity. For the legs, I'm planning to attach them underneath the hut via sill beams around y 2.0-2.15, with hip joints at x ±0.7, using knuckle-like pads to connect the legs to the body.

Now I'm designing the feather trousers covering the thighs with tufted feathers in two alternating colors down to the scaled tarsus, adding spur details and knobby joints, then mapping out toe segments with knuckle spheres and talon claws, including a rear toe. I'm roughing out approximate joint positions and bone direction vectors for the hip and knee on one side, planning to mirror them for the opposite leg.

Continuing the leg chain down through the ankle to the foot, calculating directions so the toes sit at the right height relative to the base platform without clipping through it, adjusting the foot and toe centerline y-values slightly to get the geometry to sink in naturally.

That naming works, with kneeL as the forward bend and ankleL as the hock joint. For remaining joints, I'll add a door hinge parented to the hut, skip shutters as joints since they're minor, and settle on 18 total joints with static scenery parts like roof and ground riding on the main hut joint.

For the root structure, I'm rethinking this though—attaching ground directly to the hut joint means moving the hut would move the ground too, which breaks animation. Better to add a separate "base" joint at the origin as the true root, with "hut" as its child, so ground and static props ride the base while legs and hips parent off the hut. This brings the joint count to 19, with legs driven through an IK chain under the hut for walking.

Now I'm working out mount points and part-to-joint assignments: hutBody rides hut/door, roof rides hut, baseFence rides base, props (including the porch cat) ride base and hut. I'm calculating specific mount coordinates—ground top, hut base, floor top, wall top, ridge line extents along z, and eave positions—to anchor each geometric piece correctly to its parent joint.

Working out hip rafters and feet positions, then placing windows on both side walls at two heights (z ±0.65, y 2.85) for added richness, and setting up front and back gable positions.

Now placing the gable window centered at the top front, and the konyok (ridge decoration) fore and aft. I'm calculating the chimney position on the roof slope accounting for the slope angle, making sure its height and the smoke puffs above it stay within the overall size limit, which pushes me to bump up the total height to 5.3 and adjust the birch tree height to 4.8.

I'm setting up the overall bounding size, then figuring out the fence ring radius and gate post positions using the slope geometry so the gate opening lines up with the front path and steps, placing taller carved posts with skull and folk-cap decorations at the gate opening.

Then I extend that path outward to the stone edge, and define the base disc using a 16-gon lathe shape with a grassy top and earthen rim so the whole platform spans about 6.8 units across. For props, I'm placing a Baba Yaga-style mortar with pestle and broom off to one side, giving it a stone texture with folk-pattern details.

I briefly consider adding a black cat with glowing eyes on the porch, but after checking the tight clearance against the stairs and door, I decide it's simpler to skip the cat.

Instead I'm fleshing out the surrounding scenery: fly agaric mushrooms, folk-stylized flowers with flat petals, grass tufts, ferns, stones, and maybe a crow on a gatepost. For the fence, I'm planning stake posts topped with glowing-eyed bone skulls arranged along an arc at radius 3.0 spanning roughly 40 to 320 degrees azimuth, spacing them about 0.42m apart for around 35 posts, each skull built from several parts.

That's too many parts, so I'm cutting it down to roughly 26-30 posts spaced closer to 0.49-0.56m apart, simplifying each skull to just cranium, jaw, two eye glows, and a nose to keep the part count manageable since merging is optional below the 1000-part threshold. I'm tallying up budgets across legs, hut body, roof, fence, and props to confirm the total stays under the 900-part ceiling, and noting the glow-eye skulls need the proper glow import path.

I'm now sketching the log cabin wall construction in detail — stacking seven rows of horizontal logs between y=2.15 and 3.55, deciding how front/back versus side wall logs should span different x/z ranges with slight protrusion at the corners to simulate notched joinery, alternating which walls get the longer overhang at each row.

I'm also planning a filler wall box inside to prevent gaps showing through, log-end caps with ring details for realism, and now moving on to designing a carved folk-style door with dark plank wood, decorative red/yellow bands, hinges, and a round iron handle.

For the roof, I'm working out a shingle-row builder with alternating scalloped tile colors, carved bargeboards with cutout patterns and a hanging "polotentse" pendant at the gable peak, carved horse-head ridge ends (konyok), a sun rosette, and chimney bricks with smoke -- all needing precise slope geometry to tie together correctly.

Calculating leg box coordinates to make sure they don't collide with the stairs box, checking the toe positions against the stairs' x-range.

I'm confirming the hutBody box shares a mounting region with the legs around the hip area, then setting the final bounding boxes for the hut body and roof.

Adding the ridge, chimney, and smoke extents to the roof box, then defining the fence and prop bounding regions. I'm sketching birch trees next, using a smooth white trunk with ink dashes, simple branches, and stylized flat leaf clusters in a folk-art style.

Now I'm positioning two birches so their canopies don't collide with the roofline or fence edges, checking the x/z extents against the box boundaries, and settling on a consistent tree height around 4.7 before moving on to placing the mortar and other props along the left side.

I need to avoid the hut footprint and path/stairs zones when placing decorations. For style, I'm settling on Slavic folk art motifs: sun rosettes with petals, scalloped bargeboards, fish-scale shingles, rooster details, tulip flowers, and checker trim, plus a tree-of-life on the door. Now I'm drafting the actual JSON structure with joints and parent relationships.

Working out the leg and toe joint positions and directions for both sides (mirrored for left/right), making sure the toe tip extents stay within the bounding box and that the hip height aligns with the hut root.

For the leg builds, I'm planning feathered thighs with overlapping blade layers tapering into a scaly tarsus with ridge plates, hock spur, and clawed toes, plus folk-art touches like red anklet bands with yellow dots and a bit of mud texture near the feet.

I'm planning to build both legs using the already-created joints, favoring rigid rods or capsules swept along explicit bone paths rather than skinned meshes to keep things simpler and more compact.

Mapping out the joint chain from hip to toes with their coordinates per side, then sweeping the thigh and shin as tapered tubes bound to their respective bones, with feather-like spikes arranged radially around the thigh and a ruff of longer spikes at the knee for detail.

Still building geometry details...

I'm sanity-checking the hip and thigh placement against the box height limit, adjusting the sphere radius and start position so the cap doesn't poke through the hut ceiling, settling on starting the thigh path a bit below the hip joint.

Now I'm moving to writing the actual construction code, using vector positions for each body part with simple directional arrays, keeping the types loose for flexibility.
